meta.title: The retail price cap
meta.subtitle: Why a fall in the wholesale price does not show up on a household bill for months — and why the cap is not a cap on your bill.
meta.one_line: Ofgem sets a maximum unit rate and standing charge for households on a default tariff. It caps the RATES, not the bill, and it is built from a cost stack whose wholesale part is measured months before it takes effect.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Everything on this page is a published feature of GB retail regulation. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears here.
meta.no_current_level: This page deliberately carries NO current cap level. Ofgem resets it every quarter, so any figure written here would be wrong within weeks and would look authoritative while being so. The mechanism below does not change quarterly; the number does. For the number, go to Ofgem.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem's published cap guidance and its 2022 decision to move to quarterly updates
claim_freshness.route: Read in a browser by a person. Ofgem's cap pages render their content with JavaScript and return only navigation to this project's fetch tooling, so an automated check is not currently possible and a human read is the route that works.
claims_checked: The cap is not a cap on the maximum bill -- Ofgem states this plainly.
The headline level represents a typical dual-fuel customer at typical consumption (TDCV).
The lag is real: Ofgem moved to quarterly updates in 2022 expressly 'so prices don't lag behind changes in the market'.
claim_freshness.note: Written 2026-08-18 from established regulatory mechanism; the two core claims above were then checked against Ofgem's own published material and hold.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: The price cap is a ceiling on what a supplier may charge per unit of energy and per day for standing charge, for households who have never switched or whose fixed deal has ended — and because the wholesale part of that ceiling is measured over a window that closes before the cap period begins, the cap moves months after the market it is following.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Two things are widely believed about the cap and both are wrong. The first is that it caps your bill. It does not: it caps the PRICE of each unit and the daily standing charge. Use twice as much energy and you pay roughly twice as much, capped or not. The figure quoted in the news is what a household with typical consumption would pay over a year at the capped rates — an illustration, not a limit. A household that uses more than typical will pay more than the headline, and has not been overcharged.

The second is that the cap tracks the market. It follows it, at a distance. Ofgem looks at wholesale prices over an observation window, then sets a cap for a period that starts after that window has closed. So when gas prices collapse, capped bills stay high for months; when they spike, capped bills stay low for months, and suppliers absorb the difference. The lag runs in both directions, and it is a deliberate feature — a cap that moved daily would be no more predictable for a household than no cap at all. It is also acknowledged by the regulator: when Ofgem moved the cap from six-monthly to quarterly updates in 2022, it gave the reason plainly — so that prices “don't lag behind changes in the market”. Shortening the cadence reduced the lag; it did not remove it, because the wholesale allowance is still measured over a window that closes before the period it sets.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
The cap is built up, not handed down. Ofgem constructs an allowance for each cost a supplier genuinely faces, and the cap is their sum:

• The WHOLESALE allowance — the cost of buying the energy itself. This is the largest and most volatile part, and it is derived from observed forward market prices over a defined window, on the assumption that a prudent supplier hedges ahead rather than buying on the day.

• NETWORK costs — the regulated charges for using the wires and pipes, which are set through a separate price-control process and vary by region. This is why the cap is not one number nationally.

• POLICY costs — the environmental and social obligations that are recovered through bills rather than taxation: renewables support, the obligation to insulate homes, the warm home discount.

• OPERATING costs — running a supply business: billing, metering, the contact centre, bad debt.

• An EBIT allowance — a margin for the supplier, historically in the low single digits of revenue. This is the number most often misread. A supply business operating exactly at the cap is not a high-margin business.

Each allowance is set for a TYPICAL household's consumption, then expressed as a unit rate and a standing charge. The standing charge carries the costs that do not vary with how much you use — and that is why using less energy does not reduce your bill proportionally, and why the standing charge is the most contested part of the design.

The cap is a MAXIMUM, not a target and not a price. A supplier may charge less, and in a competitive market some do. When wholesale costs sit far below the cap, the gap is where competition reappears; when they sit near it, the market converges on the cap and switching offers dry up.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
If the mechanism above is real, three things follow, and each is checkable against published data rather than taken on trust.

FIRST, capped rates should look like a lagged, smoothed version of the wholesale curve — the same shape, later and flatter. Sharp wholesale spikes should appear in the cap as broader, lower humps, arriving after the spike itself has passed.

SECOND, the gap between capped rates and current wholesale cost should swing through zero rather than sitting on one side. In a falling market the cap is above cost and suppliers earn more than the allowance; in a rising market it is below and they lose money. A cap that were consistently generous or consistently punitive would mean the observation window was mis-specified, not that the market was unusual.

THIRD, the number of fixed tariffs available below the cap should rise as the gap between wholesale cost and the cap widens, and collapse to nothing as it closes. The availability of a better deal is a direct read-out of that gap.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body: NOT SHOWN ON THIS PAGE YET, and stated rather than quietly omitted. Two of the page's core claims have been CHECKED against Ofgem's own published material -- that the cap is not a cap on the bill, and that the headline level describes a typical household at typical consumption -- and the lag has the regulator's own stated reason behind it. Checked is not the same as shown: what does not exist yet is the capped-rate series to plot against the wholesale series this site already carries, which needs Ofgem's published cap levels ingested as the files they are published as. Until that lands, the shape argued above is argued, not demonstrated.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
The wholesale allowance's exact construction — the length and placement of the observation window, and the hedging profile it assumes — is the part of the methodology that most affects the lag, and this page describes it in general terms rather than reproducing it. Anyone reasoning about the precise timing of pass-through needs Ofgem's own methodology document, not this page.

Prepayment and Economy 7 households sit under related but distinct arrangements that this page does not cover. Nor does it cover the temporary adjustments and recovery mechanisms introduced after the 2021–22 supplier failures, which materially changed the cap's level for several periods and are a significant part of why bills behaved as they did.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not carry a current cap level, deliberately — see the note above; the level changes quarterly and the mechanism does not. It does not plot capped rates against wholesale cost, which is the single thing that would turn the lag from an assertion into a demonstration. Its two core claims have been checked against Ofgem's published material, but the METHODOLOGY -- the exact construction of the wholesale allowance -- has not been read line by line, so the precise timing of pass-through should be taken from Ofgem's own document rather than from here.
